lines.text: From a Japanese master's sketchbooks to Sunday strips, caped heroes, robot boys and streaming hits, this is the story of comics, manga and anime.
It starts with Katsushika Hokusai, the Japanese artist of The Great Wave, who never stopped drawing everything he saw.
From 1814 his sketchbooks were printed as the Hokusai Manga, and the word manga came to mean Japanese comics.
In New York in the 1890s, a bald kid in a yellow nightshirt started talking in speech balloons, and the comic strip was born.
A decade later, Winsor McCay sent little Nemo into the dream kingdom of Slumberland every week, in some of the most beautiful pages ever drawn.
Then came Krazy Kat, a cat in love with a brick-throwing mouse, a strip so clever that cartoonists still study it.
In 1917, the first Japanese animated films were made. Anime would take decades to grow, and then take over the world.
In 1928 Osamu Tezuka was born. Trained as a doctor, he became the god of manga, shaping how it looks to this day.
A year later in Belgium, Herge sent a young reporter called Tintin and his dog Snowy off on adventures in more than seventy languages.
In America, a new publisher appeared that took its name from Detective Comics. DC was about to change everything.
In June 1938, Action Comics number one showed a man lifting a car over his head. Today a copy sells for millions.
He was Superman, created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, an alien raised in Kansas, and the very first superhero.
Across the Atlantic that same year, The Beano arrived in Britain, home of Dennis the Menace and the longest-running weekly comic in the world.
A year later came Batman, a rich man of Gotham with no powers at all, just a bat costume and a long list of villains.
Also in 1939, a company called Timely Comics opened its doors. One day it would be known as Marvel.
In Tokyo in 1941, Hayao Miyazaki was born, the boy who would grow up to make the world's most loved animated films.
That same year, Captain America burst onto his first cover, punching Adolf Hitler on the jaw.
And Wonder Woman arrived, an Amazon princess with a lasso of truth, still the best-known superheroine of all.
In 1950 Charles Schulz began Peanuts, with Charlie Brown, Lucy and Snoopy, and it ran for nearly fifty years.
In Japan, Tezuka created Astro Boy, a robot boy with a human heart, who later became the star of television's first big anime series.
But in America, a 1954 book claimed comics harmed children. Senate hearings followed, and a strict code tamed American comics for years.
In France, Asterix and his Gaulish village held out against the Romans with a magic potion, and readers in over a hundred languages cheered.
In 1961 Stan Lee and Jack Kirby made the Fantastic Four, heroes who bickered like a real family, and the Marvel universe began.
The next year came Spider-Man, a teenager with spider powers and very ordinary problems: school, money and guilt.
Then the X-Men, mutants born with powers and feared for being different, a story many read as one about prejudice.
In 1968, Weekly Shonen Jump launched in Japan, the magazine where many of the world's best-selling comics would first appear.
A year later came Doraemon, a robot cat from the future with a pocket full of gadgets, loved by children all over Asia.
In 1974 Sanrio drew a little white cat with a red bow. Hello Kitty went on to appear on thousands of products.
Then Garfield, the fat, lazy, lasagne-loving cat, who became the most widely syndicated comic strip in the world.
Comics were growing up. In Maus, Art Spiegelman drew his father's survival of the Holocaust, and it won a special Pulitzer Prize.
In Japan, Katsuhiro Otomo's Akira tore through a ruined Tokyo, and its 1988 film opened Western eyes to anime.
In 1984 Akira Toriyama began Dragon Ball, and Goku's hunt for the magic balls helped carry manga and anime around the globe.
The next year, Miyazaki, Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki founded Studio Ghibli.
In America, Calvin and his tiger Hobbes shared ten years of wild adventures, and their creator refused to sell a single toy.
In 1986 Frank Miller brought an ageing Batman out of retirement in a grim future, and Batman stayed dark for decades.
That same year, Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons' Watchmen showed tired heroes on the edge of nuclear war, and adults took comics seriously.
In 1991 Sailor Moon turned a schoolgirl into a warrior protecting the Earth, and magical girls charmed the world.
Then Detective Conan, a teenage sleuth shrunk to a child, began solving mysteries, and he has not stopped since.
In 1995 Neon Genesis Evangelion put teenagers inside giant machines, then turned deep into their troubled minds.
In 1996 two Game Boy games came out in Japan, and Pokemon, with its creatures to catch and battle, became a worldwide craze.
A year later Luffy and his pirate crew set sail in One Piece, the best-selling manga of all time.
Then Naruto, a young ninja dreaming of leading his village, ran for fifteen years and won fans everywhere.
In 2000 Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis told of growing up in Iran after the revolution, in simple black and white.
And in 2001 Miyazaki's Spirited Away, about a girl in a bathhouse for spirits, won the Oscar for best animated feature.
In 2003 The Walking Dead began its long march of zombies and survivors, later a hit on television.
That year also brought Death Note, about a student who finds a notebook that kills anyone whose name is written in it.
In 2008 Iron Man opened a chain of linked Marvel films that became the highest-grossing film series ever.
A year later, Attack on Titan trapped the last humans behind giant walls, hiding from man-eating giants.
In 2016 Demon Slayer began, a boy hunting demons to save his sister, and it soon became a national craze in Japan.
That summer, Pokemon Go sent millions of people walking through real streets to catch creatures on their phones.
Also in 2016, Makoto Shinkai's Your Name, about a boy and a girl who swap bodies, became a huge hit across Asia.
In 2018 Black Panther took audiences to the hidden kingdom of Wakanda, the first superhero film nominated for best picture.
That same year, Jujutsu Kaisen began, a schoolboy who swallows a cursed finger, and one of the biggest series of the decade.
In 2020, with cinemas half closed by the pandemic, Demon Slayer Mugen Train became Japan's highest-grossing film ever.
And in 2023 Miyazaki returned with The Boy and the Heron, and won his second Oscar.
From a sketchbook in Edo to screens everywhere, the pictures keep telling stories.
